---
title: "First Suffolk Senate: Nick Collins faces a Wu-backed primary challenge"
description: |
    Boston Mayor Michelle Wu's endorsement of Latoya Gayle sets up a high-profile
    primary challenge to incumbent Senator Nick Collins in a First Suffolk district
    that redistricting has quietly remade.
author: Brent Benson
date: 2026-07-22
image: /images/first-suffolk-map.png
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(gtExtras)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(formattable)

tmap_mode("view")
```

```{r}
# National two-election average (2024 + 2020) for PVI baseline
US_Harris_24 <- 75017626
US_Trump_24  <- 77301997
US_Biden_20  <- 81281502
US_Trump_20  <- 74222593
US_PVI_24 <- (US_Harris_24 + US_Biden_20) /
             (US_Harris_24 + US_Trump_24 + US_Biden_20 + US_Trump_20)

pvi_string <- function(pvi_n) {
    case_when(
        pvi_n <= -0.5 ~ str_c("R+", round(abs(pvi_n))),
        pvi_n >= 0.5  ~ str_c("D+", round(pvi_n)),
        TRUE          ~ "EVEN"
    )
}

prec_data <- read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bwbensonjr/mapoli/refs/heads/master/pvi/ma_precincts_districts_pres_2024.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
)

prec_demographics <- read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bwbensonjr/mapoli/refs/heads/master/demographics/data/ma_precinct_demographics.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
    select(
        city_town, ward, precinct, wwc_pct, race_white_pct, ed_college_degree_pct,
        total_population, race_white, race_black, race_hispanic, race_asian,
        race_multiracial, median_household_income
    )

first_suffolk_data <- prec_data |>
    filter(State_Senate == "First Suffolk") |>
    left_join(prec_demographics, by = c("city_town", "ward", "precinct")) |>
    filter(!is.na(wwc_pct)) |>
    mutate(
        PVI_N         = ((Harris_24 + Biden_20) /
                         (Harris_24 + Trump_24 + Biden_20 + Trump_20) - US_PVI_24) * 100,
        PVI           = pvi_string(PVI_N),
        WWC_PCT       = wwc_pct * 100,
        WWC_PCT_clamped = pmin(WWC_PCT, 30),
        WHITE_PCT     = race_white_pct * 100,
        COLLEGE_PCT   = ed_college_degree_pct * 100,
        # Mutually-exclusive race/ethnicity shares (sum ~100%); Native American,
        # Hawaiian, and Other are negligible district-wide so are omitted here.
        BLACK_PCT     = race_black / total_population * 100,
        HISP_PCT      = race_hispanic / total_population * 100,
        ASIAN_PCT     = race_asian / total_population * 100,
        MULTI_PCT     = race_multiracial / total_population * 100,
        plurality_idx = max.col(
            as.matrix(pick(WHITE_PCT, BLACK_PCT, HISP_PCT, ASIAN_PCT, MULTI_PCT)),
            ties.method = "first"
        ),
        PLURALITY = factor(
            c("White", "Black", "Hispanic", "Asian", "Multiracial")[plurality_idx],
            levels = c("White", "Black", "Hispanic", "Asian", "Multiracial")
        ),
        HH_INCOME         = median_household_income,
        HH_INCOME_clamped = pmin(HH_INCOME, 250000),
        # Diversity-Affluence Index: income percentile (relative to the district)
        # times the normalized Shannon diversity of the five race/ethnicity shares.
        # It peaks where a precinct is both racially mixed AND high-income -- the
        # gentrification signature -- and stays low for affluent-but-white South
        # Boston or diverse-but-lower-income Dorchester.
        AFF_PCTILE = percent_rank(HH_INCOME),
        SHANNON = pmap_dbl(
            list(WHITE_PCT, BLACK_PCT, HISP_PCT, ASIAN_PCT, MULTI_PCT),
            function(w, b, h, a, m) {
                ps <- c(w, b, h, a, m) / 100
                ps <- ps[ps > 0]
                -sum(ps * log(ps)) / log(5)
            }
        ),
        DIV_AFF = round(AFF_PCTILE * SHANNON * 100, 1),
        precinct_label = if_else(ward == "-", precinct, str_c(ward, "-", precinct))
    )
```

On September 1, Democratic primary voters in the First Suffolk
district will decide whether to send state Senator Nick Collins back
to Beacon Hill for another term or to nominate one of two Democratic
challengers. The higher-profile challenger is Latoya Gayle, a
first-time candidate backed by Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, making this a
proxy war between Wu and one of her most persistent legislative
antagonists.

Collins, a South Boston Democrat who has held the seat since a 2018
special election, is a conservative voice representing a portion of
the much more progressive City of Boston. Gayle, 47, a Dorchester
resident and advocacy director at the early-education nonprofit
Neighborhood Villages, entered as a political newcomer and picked up
Wu's endorsement on [June 3](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/06/03/metro/wu-endorses-gayle-collins-state-senate/).
A third Democrat, Juwan Skeens—who lost to Collins in 2024—is also
on the ballot, raising some concerns about progressive vote splitting.

Mayor Wu and Senator Collins have clashed publicly, chiefly over her
push to shift more of Boston's property-tax burden onto commercial
real estate, a measure Collins repeatedly helped block in the
Senate. Her backing came with two labor unions (SEIU and AFSCME
Local 703) and political experience—Gayle's campaign manager
previously worked in Wu's City Hall.

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| tbl-cap: |
#|   *The three Democrats on the September 1 ballot in the First Suffolk.*

tribble(
    ~candidate, ~background, ~raised_2026, ~cash_on_hand,
    "Nick Collins",
        "Incumbent since 2018. South Boston; former state representative and a conservative Democrat in a progressive-led Senate.",
        246711.71, 100567.72,
    "Latoya Gayle",
        "First-time candidate from Dorchester; advocacy director at the nonprofit Neighborhood Villages. Endorsed by Mayor Wu, SEIU, and AFSCME Local 703.",
        49560.05, 18760.46,
    "Juwan Skeens",
        "Former staffer to Attorney General Andrea Campbell; challenged Collins in 2024, losing by better than three to one.",
        48.02, 35.30
) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(
        candidate     = "Candidate",
        background    = "Background",
        raised_2026   = "Raised in 2026",
        cash_on_hand  = "Cash on hand"
    ) |>
    fmt_currency(c(raised_2026, cash_on_hand), decimals = 0) |>
    cols_width(
        candidate    ~ pct(18),
        background   ~ pct(52),
        raised_2026  ~ pct(15),
        cash_on_hand ~ pct(15)
    ) |>
    tab_source_note(
        md("*Year-to-date receipts and ending cash on hand as of June 30, 2026 (Massachusetts Office of Campaign and Political Finance).*")
    ) |>
    tab_options(
        table.font.size = px(14),
        table.width = pct(100)
    )
```

The fundamentals favor the incumbent. Collins has out-raised Gayle by roughly
five to one this year and held about \$100,000 in cash at the end of June to
Gayle's \$19,000. An internal poll his campaign circulated in June showed him
ahead 82 percent to Gayle's 10 and Skeens's 9—a figure to treat with the
skepticism any internal poll deserves, but a plausible signal of the name
recognition an eight-year incumbent carries into a low-turnout September primary.

But the First Suffolk district has changed a great deal from the one
Collins first won in 2018. The four maps below portray the district's
demographics as they stand today, and the trend lines that follow show
how sharply—and how recently—those demographics have changed.

## White Working-Class

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *White working-class share of each First Suffolk precinct*

# Boston mainland boundary to clip the precinct polygons. The generalized
# coastline layer counts the harbor islands as land, but they have no voters,
# so we keep only the largest connected component (the mainland).
boston_land <- read_sf(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bwbensonjr/mapoli/refs/heads/master/gis/geojson/city_town_2024.geojson"
) |>
    filter(city_town == "Boston") |>
    st_make_valid() |>
    st_cast("POLYGON") |>
    mutate(part_area = st_area(geometry)) |>
    slice_max(part_area, n = 1) |>
    st_geometry()

first_suffolk_geom <- read_sf(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bwbensonjr/mapoli/refs/heads/master/gis/geojson/wardsprecincts2022.geojson"
) |>
    right_join(first_suffolk_data, by = c("city_town", "ward", "precinct")) |>
    st_make_valid() |>
    st_buffer(dist = 10) |>
    st_buffer(dist = -10) |>
    st_simplify(dTolerance = 25) |>
    st_intersection(boston_land) |>
    st_make_valid()

wwc_palette <- c("#FFF7EC", "#FEE8C8", "#FDD49E", "#FDBB84", "#FC8D59", "#EF6548", "#D7301F", "#990000")

district_map <- (
    tm_shape(first_suffolk_geom) +
    tm_polygons(
        fill       = "WWC_PCT_clamped",
        fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(
            values = wwc_palette,
            limits = c(0, 30),
            ticks  = c(0, 10, 20, 30),
            labels = c("0%", "10%", "20%", "30%+")
        ),
        fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "White Working\nClass %"),
        fill_alpha  = 0.7,
        popup.vars  = c(
            "Precinct"            = "precinct_label",
            "White working class" = "WWC_PCT",
            "White %"             = "WHITE_PCT",
            "College degree %"    = "COLLEGE_PCT",
            "PVI"                 = "PVI"
        )
    ) +
    tm_basemap("OpenStreetMap")
)

district_map
```

## Race and Ethnicity

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *Largest racial or ethnic group for each precinct*

plurality_palette <- c(

    Asian       = "#6A51A3",
    Multiracial = "#969696"

race_map <- (
    tm_shape(first_suffolk_geom) +
    tm_polygons(
        fill        = "PLURALITY",
        fill.scale  = tm_scale_categorical(values = plurality_palette),
        fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Largest group"),
        fill_alpha  = 0.7,
        popup.vars  = c(
            "Precinct"      = "precinct_label",
            "Largest group" = "PLURALITY",
            "White %"        = "WHITE_PCT",
            "Black %"        = "BLACK_PCT",
            "Hispanic %"     = "HISP_PCT",
            "Asian %"        = "ASIAN_PCT",
            "Multiracial %"  = "MULTI_PCT"
        )
    ) +
    tm_basemap("OpenStreetMap")
)

race_map
```

## Diversity and Affluence

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *Diversity-Affluence Index—income percentile times racial diversity. High
#|   values flag precincts that are both racially mixed and high-income, surfacing
#|   the gentrifying neighborhoods that the race and income maps each tell only
#|   half of.*

divaff_palette <- c("#FCFBFD", "#EFEDF5", "#DADAEB", "#BCBDDC", "#9E9AC8", "#807DBA", "#6A51A3", "#4A1486")

divaff_map <- (
    tm_shape(first_suffolk_geom) +
    tm_polygons(
        fill       = "DIV_AFF",
        fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(
            values = divaff_palette,
            limits = c(0, 80),
            ticks  = c(0, 20, 40, 60, 80)
        ),
        fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Diversity-\nAffluence"),
        fill_alpha  = 0.7,
        popup.vars  = c(
            "Precinct"            = "precinct_label",
            "Div-Affluence index" = "DIV_AFF",
            "Median HH income"    = "HH_INCOME",
            "White %"             = "WHITE_PCT",
            "Largest group"       = "PLURALITY"
        )
    ) +
    tm_basemap("OpenStreetMap")
)

divaff_map
```

## How the District Has Changed

The maps above are a snapshot. But the First Suffolk district that
Nick Collins represents today is not the one his predecessors held—and
not because the neighborhoods themselves were transformed. The chart
below tracks the district's race and ethnicity using American
Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates from 2009 to 2024. The dashed
lines mark the two redistricting cycles that fall within this window.

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *Race and ethnicity of the First Suffolk Senate district, ACS 5-year
#|   estimates. Lines break at each redistricting because the district's
#|   boundaries—not just its population—changed.*

ts <- read_csv(
    "first_suffolk_demographics_timeseries.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Reuse the plurality colors from the race map for visual continuity.
race_ts_palette <- c(
    White       = "#2166AC",
    Black       = "#238B45",
    Hispanic    = "#E6550D",
    Asian       = "#6A51A3",
    Multiracial = "#969696"
)

race_long <- ts |>
    select(
        acs_endpoint_year, redistricting_cycle,
        White = white_pct, Black = black_pct, Hispanic = hispanic_pct,
        Asian = asian_pct, Multiracial = multiracial_pct
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(
        c(White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, Multiracial),
        names_to = "group", values_to = "pct"
    ) |>
    mutate(group = factor(group, levels = names(race_ts_palette)))

# Redistricting takes effect between the 2011/2012 and 2021/2022 endpoints.
redistrict_breaks <- c(2011.5, 2021.5)

ggplot(
    race_long,
    aes(
        acs_endpoint_year, pct,
        color = group,
        # Group by cycle so lines do NOT connect across a boundary change.
        group = interaction(group, redistricting_cycle)
    )
) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = redistrict_breaks, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey55") +
    annotate("text", x = 2011.5, y = 48, label = "2021 plan →",
             hjust = 1.05, size = 3, color = "grey40") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5) +
    scale_color_manual(values = race_ts_palette) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2009, 2024, 3)) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"), limits = c(0, 50)) +
    labs(x = "ACS 5-year endpoint", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The trends between redistricting map changes are gradual. Under the
2011 map (2012–2021), the district drifted slowly, with the Black share
easing from roughly 41% toward 36% as Hispanic and white-collar
residents grew. Then the lines jump discontinuously at the 2021
redistricting—White rises from about 34% to 46%, Black falls from 36%
to 21%, and Asian climbs from 8% to 13% in a single step. That break
is a **boundary effect, not a neighborhood shift**: the new map traded
Dorchester precincts for more of South Boston and the Seaport. The
2021 redistricting reshaped First Suffolk more than fifteen years of
demographic change did.

```{r}
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-cap: |
#|   *Median household income, First Suffolk Senate district (ACS 5-year,
#|   nominal dollars). The same redistricting break that whitened the district
#|   also raised its income floor.*

ggplot(ts, aes(acs_endpoint_year, median_hh_income, group = redistricting_cycle)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = redistrict_breaks, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey55") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "#238B45") +
    geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#238B45") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2009, 2024, 3)) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
    labs(x = "ACS 5-year endpoint", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Median household income climbed steadily across both eras—from under
\$50,000 in the 2005–2009 window to nearly \$113,000 in 2020–2024—but
the 2021 redistricting created a large one-time bump, lifting the figure
past \$100,000 by folding in the district's newly added wealthier
waterfront precincts.

## What September 1 Will Test

The demographic story cuts both ways for the challenger. On paper, the post-2021
map is *friendlier* to Collins than the one he first won: it is whiter,
wealthier, and more firmly anchored in South Boston and the Seaport, where his
name—and the annual St. Patrick's Day Breakfast he hosts—still carries weight.
An incumbent who has never had to sweat a general election in this seat starts
with the terrain tilted his way.

Yet the same redistricting added some unfamiliar ground. Much of the
South End—which is more progressive and has less history with
Collins—is now in the district. But Gayle will likely need to run the table
in the South End and Dorchester, especially the areas that are high on
the Diversity-Affluence scale, while limiting damage in South Boston.

Skeens raises an additional challenge. A progressive who won a couple
thousand votes against Collins in 2024, he may draw a similar number in
2026—and those are votes more likely to come at Gayle's expense than
Collins's.

Gayle is not the favorite to win in September. The money and the sheer
difficulty of unseating a Massachusetts incumbent both point the other
way. But the district Collins is defending has been shifting beneath
him—some of it slowly, but most of it in one redistricting jolt—and
Wu's endorsement is a bet that it has shifted far enough to
matter. September 1 will measure whether it has.
